name: Mucuna pruriens

card.summary: A tropical bean rich in natural L-DOPA, used in Ayurveda and sold as a dopamine, libido and testosterone supplement; human evidence exists mainly for Parkinson's disease.
card.note: Contains L-DOPA; nausea and vomiting are reported at higher intakes and MAO inhibitor users are advised to avoid it. Pod hairs cause severe itching.

quick.overview:
Mucuna pruriens is a climbing legume whose seeds contain roughly 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA, the precursor to dopamine. Ayurvedic tradition uses the seeds as a nerve tonic and aphrodisiac, and the powder is sold as a supplement for mood, motivation, libido and male fertility.

The human evidence is mainly in Parkinson's disease: a small crossover study of 8 patients found seed powder gave faster onset and longer on-time than standard levodopa/carbidopa. No human trial for appearance-related use was found; fertility and testosterone claims rest on animal studies.
quick.mechanism: L-DOPA is converted to dopamine by the enzyme aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase. Forum users discuss pairing it with other supplements to modify this pathway; in Parkinson's treatment, levodopa is combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor because much converts to dopamine outside the brain.
quick.risks: L-DOPA sensitivity can cause nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and low blood pressure, according to Wikipedia, which advises people on MAOIs to avoid the plant. A looksmax.org user reported vomiting after taking many capsules. Contact with raw pod hairs causes severe itching.

lead: Mucuna pruriens, the velvet bean, is a tropical climbing legume native to Africa and tropical Asia, grown as forage and green manure and eaten in parts of Indonesia.[1] Its seeds contain about 3 to 6 percent L-DOPA (levodopa), the dopamine precursor used in Parkinson's disease treatment, while its pod hairs contain compounds that cause intense itching.[1][2]

In looksmaxxing and biohacking circles it is a supplement people take for drive, mood and libido, on the reasoning that more dopamine means more motivation to train, eat well and keep up the habits behind a better physique and presentation.[3][4] Traditional Indian and African medicine uses the seeds as an aphrodisiac, nervine tonic and remedy for male infertility and Parkinsonian conditions.[5]

Human research is concentrated in Parkinson's disease, where several small randomized trials have compared seed powder with standard levodopa preparations, beginning with a 2004 crossover study of eight patients.[6][7][8] No published human trial has tested mucuna for motivation, appearance or testosterone in healthy people; fertility findings come from animal studies.[9]

angle.goal: Drive and mood (for training and self-care)
chain: Users hope for more motivation and mood, supporting training and routine
angle.text: Mucuna is discussed as an over-the-counter dopamine source. Looksmaxxing posters take it with the aim of more drive and mood, which they link to sticking with training, diet and grooming; the appearance effect is indirect and rests on that motivation chain.

paras: Mucuna pruriens is an annual climbing vine that can exceed 15 metres, with white, lavender or purple flowers in long clusters and pods 4 to 13 cm long covered in orange hairs, each holding up to seven shiny seeds.[1] It is widely naturalised in the tropics and is invasive in parts of South Florida.[1]

Seeds contain roughly 3.1 to 6.1 percent L-DOPA, with a cited range of 3 to 7 percent of dry weight, and very small amounts of tryptamines.[1] Wikipedia notes that about half of the L-DOPA in seeds was found to degrade into reactive compounds, and the plant's role as a source of the amino acid has been reviewed in plant biology as well as medicine.[1][10] Grokipedia describes seeds as 20 to 30 percent protein and says commercial supplements vary widely in L-DOPA content.[2]

The pod hairs contain serotonin and a protein called mucunain that cause intense itching on contact, and they are used in some itching powders; for the same reason mucuna is used in experimental itch models in human volunteers.[1][11][12]

Agricultural uses include forage, fallow and green-manure crops, and as a legume it fixes nitrogen; in Indonesia the beans are eaten and fermented into a tempeh-like food.[1] In Benin and Vietnam it has been used to control the grass Imperata cylindrica.[1] Tribal communities have long used it as a snakebite remedy, according to Wikipedia.[1]

In Ayurveda and African traditional medicine the seeds are used for male infertility, nervous disorders, Parkinson's disease, diabetes and rheumatism.[5][5] Supplements sell seed powder or L-DOPA-standardised extract.

On looksmax.org, threads discuss mucuna as an over-the-counter route to dopamine. One discussion explains the biochemistry in detail, noting that L-DOPA skips the first steps of dopamine synthesis, that it is quickly decarboxylated outside the brain, and that Parkinson's treatment pairs levodopa with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor such as carbidopa; the poster proposes pairing mucuna with green tea catechins and quercetin, which they say have enzyme-inhibiting effects.[4] Replies in the same thread mention other compounds users have in mind for dopamine.[4]

Lifting and testosterone-therapy forums such as T Nation carry parallel discussions. Posters suggest mucuna or tyrosine as dopamine support when men on hormone therapy feel flat, mention using mucuna extract alongside other supplements, and several say they felt nothing from it.[14][15][16][17] One poster reported that prolactin went up on bloodwork while taking a mucuna product and wondered about it.[18]
Members who experiment report their own results. A looksmax.org member posted a self-experiment taking a very large number of capsules and reported vomiting roughly 90 to 120 minutes later.[3]

L-DOPA is decarboxylated to dopamine by aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; dopamine cannot cross the blood-brain barrier, whereas levodopa can, so conventional Parkinson's therapy adds a peripheral inhibitor such as carbidopa or benserazide.[4][19] Wikipedia notes that mucuna supplements lack such an inhibitor, so more of the L-DOPA is converted outside the brain.[19]

Seeds also contain serotonin and tryptamines, and tryptamines are normally broken down in the gut but can become active alongside monoamine oxidase inhibitors, which is why people taking MAOIs are advised to avoid the plant.[1] Reviews describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties for the seed extract in neurodegeneration models.[20]

The species was described in 1759.[1] L-DOPA itself was first synthesised in 1911 and isolated from fava beans in 1913; Arvid Carlsson's work in the 1950s on levodopa and reserpine-treated animals earned him the 2000 Nobel Prize; Hornykiewicz and Birkmayer reported benefit in patients in 1960 to 1961; George Cotzias used high oral doses in 1969; Roche marketed levodopa as Larodopa in 1970; and carbidopa was added in 1974.[19]

Parkinson's disease. A 2004 randomized, controlled, double-blind crossover study gave eight patients with Parkinson's disease single doses of levodopa/carbidopa and two doses of mucuna seed powder. The higher dose gave a faster onset and about 37 minutes (21.9 percent) longer on-time, with higher peak plasma levodopa, and no significant difference in dyskinesias; the authors called for a larger long-term trial.[6]

Later trials include a double-blind, randomized, controlled crossover study published in Neurology in 2017, a 16-week noninferiority crossover pilot in advanced Parkinson's disease in 2018, a randomized single-blind crossover pharmacokinetic trial from Asia in 2025, and a 12-month multicentre phase II trial of mucuna powder against levodopa plus a decarboxylase inhibitor in untreated patients in sub-Saharan Africa published in 2026.[21][22][8][23] A 2025 systematic review of five clinical trials with 108 participants, one rated high quality and three low, reported that findings consistently showed improvement in Parkinson's symptoms and therapy-related outcomes.[7] ClinicalTrials.gov lists a phase 2 trial of mucuna therapy in Parkinson's disease with 18 participants.[24]

Other conditions. A 2024 review of mucuna for depression compiled animal-model evidence and said clinical trials are needed.[25] Studies of fertility and testosterone have been done in animals: rat studies reported improved sperm parameters and testis histology and a rabbit study reported shorter mounting latency and improved semen measures.[9] A 2020 review of plants in male infertility lists mucuna among plants studied, noting that efforts to apply them at the clinical level have been limited.[26]
No human randomized trial of mucuna for motivation, libido, testosterone or appearance outcomes in healthy people has been published.

Wikipedia reports that people sensitive to L-DOPA may experience nausea, vomiting, cramping, arrhythmias and hypotension, and advises that people taking monoamine oxidase inhibitors avoid the plant.[1] Grokipedia lists nausea, insomnia, bloating, hallucinations or psychosis at high or prolonged intake and says the plant is contraindicated in pregnancy, breastfeeding and low blood pressure.[2]

For levodopa generally, adverse effects include hypertension, hallucinations, confusion and sleep disturbance, and long-term use brings wearing-off, dyskinesia and dopamine dysregulation syndrome.[19] A 2025 case report series describes dopamine dysregulation syndrome in Parkinson's disease.[27] A looksmax.org user reported vomiting about 90 to 120 minutes after taking a large number of capsules.[3] The pod hairs cause dermatitis and severe itch.[1]

Mucuna is sold as a dietary supplement in the US, in capsules and powders that are marketed around L-DOPA content for mood, motivation and libido, and a US drug label lists mucuna fruit trichome in a topical itch product.[2][13] On forums it sits among dopamine-oriented supplements and is often recommended alongside tyrosine, with reports ranging from a perceived lift to no effect.[4][14][16]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org mucuna is discussed as an over-the-counter dopamine and drive supplement, and users share self-experiments including reports of side effects; lifting forums add reports of little or no effect.[3][4][14]

claims.claim: Mucuna pruriens is a way to "dopamine max" because it contains L-DOPA
claims.believers: Forum proponents note that it contains the dopamine precursor L-DOPA and can be bought without a prescription, and discuss stacking it with green tea extract and quercetin to slow dopamine breakdown.[4]
claims.experts: Mucuna seed powder has been tested against levodopa/carbidopa in small Parkinson's studies, where it raised plasma levodopa; no published human study has tested it as a mood, drive or appearance supplement.[6][7]

claims.claim: Mucuna lifts mood for men feeling flat on hormone therapy
claims.believers: T Nation posters suggest mucuna or tyrosine to support dopamine.[14][17]
claims.experts: A 2024 review of mucuna in depression compiled animal-model evidence and said clinical trials are needed.[25]

claims.believers: Several T Nation posters say they got no effect from mucuna or tyrosine.[15][16]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes mucuna supplements lack a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor, so more of the L-DOPA is converted outside the brain.[19]

claims.believers: One user posted a self-experiment reporting vomiting roughly 90 to 120 minutes after taking many capsules.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia lists nausea and vomiting among effects in people sensitive to L-DOPA.[1]

claims.claim: Mucuna can raise or lower prolactin
claims.believers: A T Nation poster noted a prolactin rise on bloodwork while taking a mucuna product and found it surprising.[18]
claims.experts: No published human trial has measured prolactin in healthy mucuna users.

claims.claim: Mucuna boosts libido and male fertility
claims.believers: Proponents cite traditional Ayurvedic use as an aphrodisiac and fertility tonic.[5]
claims.experts: Animal studies report improved sperm and testis measures; no human randomized trial has been published.[9][26]

claims.claim: Mucuna is a safe herbal alternative to a drug
claims.believers: Supplement users note it is a plant and sold over the counter.[4]
claims.experts: It contains L-DOPA, which is linked to nausea, hypotension, arrhythmia and, with long-term use, dopamine dysregulation syndrome; people on MAOIs are advised to avoid it.[1][19][27]
